client: I got promoted about six weeks ago, and honestly, I thought I'd feel good about it, but instead I just feel like I'm drowning. Every day I go in and I'm convinced that everyone around me is going to figure out that I don't actually deserve to be there. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the pressure is real and it doesn't just go away because I understand it better.
therapist: What you're describing — that constant dread of being "found out" — has a name: impostor syndrome, and it's incredibly common after a real achievement like a promotion, even though that doesn't make it feel any less exhausting. I hear your skepticism about whether talking will help, and that's a fair thing to hold onto, but what CBT can do is help us examine whether the story your mind is telling you — that you *don't* deserve to be there — actually holds up against the evidence. What would you say are some of the concrete reasons your employer decided *you* were the right person for this role?

client: I mean... I know they said it was because of the Henderson project, and how I handled the team restructuring last spring. But honestly, when I think about those things, my brain immediately jumps to "yeah, but that was luck" or "anyone could have done that." It's like no matter what evidence I try to bring up, there's this voice that just... dismantles it before it even lands.
therapist: That "yeah, but" voice is so sneaky — it lets the evidence in just long enough to immediately neutralize it, which keeps you stuck in the same loop no matter how much you logically know. In CBT we'd call this a cognitive distortion called *discounting the positive*, and the important thing to notice is that the voice isn't neutral or objective — it's applying a completely different standard to your successes than it would to, say, a colleague's. If a teammate had led the Henderson project and handled that restructuring, would *you* write it off as luck, or would you see it as genuine skill?

client: Okay, that's... actually a fair point, and it kind of stops me in my tracks a little. If it were my colleague Sarah who'd done all that, I'd probably be genuinely impressed and think she really knew what she was doing. But when I try to apply that same thinking to myself, it just feels like I'm making excuses or being arrogant, like I'm not allowed to claim credit the way I would give it to someone else.
therapist: That moment of recognition you just had is really significant — you've caught your mind operating with a double standard in real time, where extending credit to yourself feels forbidden in a way it simply doesn't for others. It's worth gently questioning where that rule came from — the idea that acknowledging your own competence equals arrogance — because that belief is doing a lot of heavy lifting in keeping the impostor feelings alive. What do you think taught you that claiming credit for yourself was something to be ashamed of?

client: I think it probably came from growing up in a house where if you talked about doing well at something, someone would always cut you down or say you were getting too big for your boots. So I learned pretty early that it was safer to just... not claim anything, stay small, keep quiet about any wins. But even knowing that now, sitting here, it still feels really uncomfortable to think about just... allowing myself to say "I did that well" without immediately bracing for some kind of punishment.
therapist: What you just shared takes real courage — you've traced this all the way back to its roots, and it makes complete sense that a rule learned so young, in a place where it genuinely protected you, would still feel carved into you even when the environment has completely changed. The discomfort you feel around claiming credit isn't a character flaw — it's actually a very loyal, well-practiced protective instinct that just hasn't gotten the update that you're no longer in that house. I'm curious — what do you imagine might happen, right now in your life, if you allowed yourself to say out loud: "I handled that restructuring well, and I earned this promotion"?

client: I sit with that question for a moment, and honestly, my stomach tightens just hearing it repeated back to me like that. I think... I'm afraid people would see me as arrogant, or that someone would come along and prove me wrong, like I'd jinxed myself by saying it out loud. It's almost like staying quiet about it has been my way of keeping it safe, keeping it real, if that makes any sense.
therapist: That makes complete sense, and there's something really poignant about the idea that staying small has felt like the only way to protect something precious — like speaking your success aloud might shatter it. But I want to gently point out that what you're describing is essentially a superstition your mind has built: that silence is a shield, when really it's been quietly costing you the ability to stand firmly in something you genuinely earned. What might it feel like to separate those two things — the fear of others' reactions, and the private, internal truth that you did this well — and just let that second one exist, even quietly, for yourself?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me actually wants to believe that's possible — like, just holding it privately without needing anyone else to validate it or tear it down. But honestly, separating the two feels almost impossible in practice, because the moment I start to feel proud, my brain immediately jumps to imagining someone rolling their eyes or saying I got lucky. It's like the fear is just... built into the feeling itself, I can't find where one ends and the other begins.
therapist: What you're describing — pride and fear being so fused together that they feel like a single thing — makes a lot of sense given what you've shared about where you grew up, because you learned them at the same time, as a package deal. The good news is that things that got wired together through experience can also, slowly, be separated through new experiences — and what we're doing right now, noticing the pattern without the sky falling in, is actually a small version of that. I wonder if this week you might try something small: when you notice that pride-fear fusion arise, just pause and ask yourself "whose voice is actually rolling their eyes right now — someone here, or someone from a long time ago?"

client: That question actually stopped me for a second, because I think I know the answer — it's almost always someone from a long time ago, probably my dad. But here's what worries me about trying that in the moment: I'm not sure I'll have the presence of mind to pause and ask anything, because when that feeling hits, it's so fast and so physical that I'm already in it before I even realize what's happening. It feels less like a thought I can catch and more like a reflex I can't.
therapist: That insight about your dad is really important, and it's okay that it comes with some worry — you're not dismissing the work, you're being honest about how deeply ingrained this reflex is, which is actually a sign of real self-awareness. You're right that catching a thought mid-spiral is hard, which is why in CBT we often work *after* the moment rather than during it — so instead of intercepting the reflex in real time, you might just notice it once the wave has passed and ask yourself then, "whose voice was that?" What do you think it would mean for you, even gradually, to start recognizing your dad's presence in those moments — even just in hindsight?

client: I think recognizing his voice in hindsight might actually be something I could try, because in the moment I'm just too flooded to think clearly. But I'm a little worried that even after the fact, I'll just end up feeling guilty about the whole thing — like, "great, now I know it was his voice, so what, I still acted like a failure." I'm not sure how noticing it actually changes anything for me.
therapist: That worry makes a lot of sense — noticing a pattern without knowing what to do with it can feel like being handed a map with no destination, and I don't want this to become just another way your mind finds to criticize yourself. The shift we're aiming for isn't "now I know better so I should have done better" — it's much gentler than that, more like slowly becoming a compassionate witness to yourself rather than another voice in the chorus that tears you down. What do you think it would feel like to notice "that was dad's voice" and respond to yourself the way you'd respond to Sarah in that same moment — with understanding rather than judgment?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me really wants to believe that's possible. But honestly, when I try to imagine responding to myself the way I'd respond to Sarah, it just feels... fake, almost, like I'd be lying to myself or letting myself off the hook for something. I think the part of me that sounds like my dad is also the part that genuinely believes I deserve that criticism, and I don't know how to get around that.
therapist: There's something really honest and painful in what you just said — that the critical voice doesn't just feel like an intruder, it feels like *truth*, which makes it so much harder to challenge because it's not just your dad's voice anymore, it's become your own. That's one of the most important things we can untangle here: the difference between a belief feeling true and a belief *being* true, because you absorbed that criticism at an age when you had no choice but to trust the person delivering it. I want to ask you gently — if that same critical voice had been applied to you consistently by a teacher or a stranger rather than a parent, do you think you'd find it quite so easy to believe it deserved to be trusted?

client: That's... actually a really uncomfortable question, because my first instinct is to say no, I wouldn't trust a stranger's cruelty the same way. But then there's this other part of me that immediately pushes back and says, "well, maybe a stranger would see the truth more clearly, without being biased toward loving you," which I realize even as I say it sounds like I'm defending the voice again. It's like no matter what angle you come at it from, I find a way to make the criticism feel legitimate.
therapist: What you just did in real time is remarkable — you caught yourself defending the critical voice *mid-sentence* and named it out loud, which is exactly the kind of awareness that starts to loosen its grip, even when it doesn't feel that way yet. There's something almost poignant about how hard that part of you works to keep the criticism safe and credible, because on some level, that voice has felt like a form of control — if you stay critical enough of yourself, maybe you can prevent the worst from happening. I'm curious: what do you think you'd have to give up, or what might feel at risk, if you actually stopped defending that voice and let it be wrong?
